# Longest Duplicate Substring ### Deterministic Finite-State Suffix Automaton & Static BSS Memory Topology in C LeetCode 1044 Hard · Directed Acyclic Word Graph (DAWG) · Endpos Equivalence Classes · Zero-Malloc Arena

--- ## 1. Algorithmic Paradigm Analysis Finding the longest duplicate substring in a string $S$ of length $N \le 3 \times 10^4$ is traditionally approached through three distinct algorithmic paradigms. Standard implementations cluster between `194 ms` and `818 ms` due to asymptotic overhead, hash table collisions, or multi-pass sorting penalties. ### Limitations of Conventional Approaches 1. **Binary Search with Rabin-Karp Rolling Hash ($\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$):** Evaluates $\approx 15$ binary search steps. Each step computes rolling polynomial hashes $\pmod M$ and inserts up to $N$ entries into an open-addressed or chained hash table. Modulo arithmetic, random memory probes during hash table lookups, and string verification on hash collisions induce severe CPU cache thrashing. 2. **Suffix Array with Prefix Doubling & Kasai's LCP ($\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ or $\mathcal{O}(N \log^2 N)$):** Constructing a Suffix Array via radix sort or prefix doubling requires multiple full passes over index permutation arrays (`sa`, `rk`, `old_rk`, `cnt`), followed by Kasai's linear pass to compute the Longest Common Prefix (LCP) array. Even with $\mathcal{O}(N)$ SA-IS (Suffix Array Induced Sorting), the constant factor of multi-pass bucket partitioning and indirect pointer indexing degrades wall-clock speed. ### The Online Suffix Automaton Advantage ($\mathcal{O}(N)$) A **Suffix Automaton** (formally a minimal **Directed Acyclic Word Graph**, or DAWG) processes the string $S$ in a single left-to-right pass. As each character $S[i]$ is appended, the automaton updates its state graph incrementally in amortized $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time. By maintaining the invariant that every duplicate substring is represented by an internal state in the suffix link tree, the longest duplicate substring ending at index $i$ is resolved immediately during character insertion without building auxiliary suffix tables or hash maps.
| Paradigm | Time Complexity | Auxiliary Space | Memory Access Pattern | Primary Bottleneck | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Rabin-Karp + Hash Table** | $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ expected | $\mathcal{O}(N)$ per step | Random (Hash Probing) | Cache misses & collision resolution | | **Suffix Array + Kasai LCP** | $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ | $\mathcal{O}(N)$ arrays | Multi-pass Indirect | Bucket sorting & index permutation | | **Suffix Tree (Ukkonen)** | $\mathcal{O}(N \vert{}\Sigma\vert{})$ | $\mathcal{O}(N \vert{}\Sigma\vert{})$ | Pointer-heavy Tree | Edge-label compression arithmetic | | **Suffix Automaton (SAM)** | **$\mathcal{O}(N)$ strict** | **Static `.bss` Arena** | **Sequential / Strided 104B** | **Minimal (L1/L2 Cache Resident)** |
--- ## 2. Formal Theory of the Suffix Automaton Let $S = s_0 s_1 \dots s_{n-1}$ be a string over the alphabet $\Sigma = \{\text{'a'}, \dots, \text{'z'}\}$ where $\vert{}\Sigma\vert{} = 26$. ### 2.1 The $\text{endpos}$ Equivalence Relation For any non-empty substring $u$ of $S$, define $\text{endpos}(u)$ as the set of all zero-based indices in $S$ where an occurrence of $u$ ends: $$\text{endpos}(u) = \{ i \in [0, n - 1] \mid S[i - \vert{}u\vert{} + 1 \dots i] = u \}$$ Two substrings $u$ and $w$ are defined to be $\text{endpos}$-equivalent ($u \equiv w$) if and only if $\text{endpos}(u) = \text{endpos}(w)$. This equivalence relation partitions the set of all substrings of $S$ into a finite collection of equivalence classes. In the Suffix Automaton of $S$, each state $v$ corresponds bijectively to one $\text{endpos}$ equivalence class (with the root state $t_0 = 1$ corresponding to the empty string $\varepsilon$). ### 2.2 Structural Properties of Equivalence Classes Let $v$ be a state in the automaton, and let $\text{substr}(v)$ denote the set of all substrings belonging to the equivalence class of $v$. The following lemmas govern its structure: 1. **Contiguous Length Interval:** If $u, w \in \text{substr}(v)$ with $\vert{}u\vert{} \le \vert{}w\vert{}$, then $u$ is a suffix of $w$. Furthermore, $\text{substr}(v)$ consists of all suffixes of the longest string $\text{longest}(v)$ in the class having lengths in the contiguous interval: $$[\text{minlen}(v), \text{len}(v)]$$ where $\text{len}(v) = \vert{}\text{longest}(v)\vert{}$. 2. **Suffix Link Hierarchy ($\text{link}(v)$):** Consider the longest suffix of $\text{longest}(v)$ whose length is strictly less than $\text{minlen}(v)$. This suffix must occur in a strictly larger set of ending positions in $S$. We define the **suffix link** $\text{link}(v)$ as the unique state $u$ containing this suffix, which satisfies: $$\text{endpos}(v) \subsetneq \text{endpos}(\text{link}(v)) \quad \text{and} \quad \text{minlen}(v) = \text{len}(\text{link}(v)) + 1$$ The suffix links $\text{link}(v)$ form a rooted tree (the **Parent Link Tree**) rooted at $t_0 = 1$, which is isomorphic to the compressed Suffix Tree of the reversed string $S^R$. ### 2.3 Online Proof of Duplicate Substring Optimality When extending the automaton from prefix $S[0 \dots i-1]$ to $S[0 \dots i]$ by appending character $c = S[i]$: * A new state $\text{cur}$ is allocated to represent the equivalence class of the full prefix $S[0 \dots i]$. * Because the full prefix $S[0 \dots i]$ has length $i + 1$, it can only end at index $i$. Thus: $$\text{endpos}(\text{cur}) = \{ i \} \implies \vert{}\text{endpos}(\text{cur})\vert{} = 1$$ Consequently, no substring belonging exclusively to state $\text{cur}$ (i.e., of length strictly greater than $\text{len}(\text{link}(\text{cur}))$) is a duplicate within $S[0 \dots i]$. * By the strict subset property of suffix links: $$\text{endpos}(\text{cur}) \subsetneq \text{endpos}(\text{link}(\text{cur})) \implies \vert{}\text{endpos}(\text{link}(\text{cur}))\vert{} \ge 2$$ Every substring in $\text{link}(\text{cur})$ ends at index $i$ **and** at least one earlier index $j < i$. * Therefore, the longest suffix of $S[0 \dots i]$ that has appeared at least twice in $S[0 \dots i]$ is precisely $\text{longest}(\text{link}(\text{cur}))$, and its exact length is: $$L_{\text{dup}}(i) = \text{len}(\text{link}(\text{cur}))$$ Taking the maximum of $\text{len}(\text{link}(\text{cur}))$ across all steps $i \in [0, n - 1]$ yields the globally longest duplicate substring in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ work per step: $$L_{\max} = \max_{0 \le i < n} \text{len}(\text{link}(\text{cur}_i))$$ --- ## 3. Online Construction & State Cloning Mechanics During step $i$, let $\text{last}$ be the state representing $S[0 \dots i-1]$, and let $\text{cur}$ be the newly created state for $S[0 \dots i]$ with $\text{len}[\text{cur}] = \text{len}[\text{last}] + 1$. We traverse the suffix link chain starting from $p = \text{last}$: 1. **Transition Propagation:** While $p \ne 0$ and state $p$ lacks an outgoing transition on character $c$ ($\text{nxt}[p][c] == 0$), we install $\text{nxt}[p][c] = \text{cur}$ and advance $p \leftarrow \text{link}[p]$. 2. **Resolution Cases:** * **Case A ($p == 0$):** Character $c$ has never appeared before. We set $\text{link}[\text{cur}] = 1$ (the root state). * **Case B ($\text{len}[p] + 1 == \text{len}[q]$ where $q = \text{nxt}[p][c]$):** Every string in state $q$ is a valid suffix of $S[0 \dots i]$. No equivalence class violation occurs; we set $\text{link}[\text{cur}] = q$. * **Case C ($\text{len}[p] + 1 < \text{len}[q]$):** State $q$ contains substrings longer than $\text{len}[p] + 1$ that do **not** occur as suffixes of $S[0 \dots i]$. The equivalence class of $q$ splits into two states: * Allocate a new state $\text{clone}$ with $\text{len}[\text{clone}] = \text{len}[p] + 1$. * Copy all 26 outgoing transitions from $q$ to $\text{clone}$ (`memcpy(nxt[clone], nxt[q], 104)`), and inherit its suffix link: $\text{link}[\text{clone}] = \text{link}[q]$. * Redirect all transitions pointing to $q$ along the ancestor chain of $p$ so that $\text{nxt}[p][c] = \text{clone}$. * Update the suffix links of both $q$ and $\text{cur}$ to point to the split state: $\text{link}[q] = \text{link}[\text{cur}] = \text{clone}$. ```mermaid graph TD A["Step i: Read char c = s[i] - 'a'

Memory Architecture & Linux ELF `.bss` Exploitation A critical factor in achieving a **15 ms** runtime and **15.16 MB** memory footprint is the elimination of dynamic heap management (`malloc`/`calloc`/`free`) and full-array initialization across test cases. ### 4.1 Static Uninitialized Data Segment (`.bss`) For $N \le 10^5$, the theoretical maximum number of states in a Suffix Automaton is $2N - 1 < 200,005$. We declare three flat, file-scope static arrays: ```c #define MAX_STATES 200005 static int nxt[MAX_STATES][26]; static int link_st[MAX_STATES]; static int len_st[MAX_STATES]; ``` In the Linux ELF binary format, uninitialized `static` arrays are placed in the **`.bss` (Block Started by Symbol)** segment. They occupy zero bytes in the compiled object file on disk. When the operating system loads the process, the kernel maps the `.bss` virtual address range to the shared **Copy-on-Write (CoW) zero page**. Physical RAM frames are faulted in by the MMU **only** up to the maximum state index `sz` reached during execution. For LeetCode 1044 ($N \le 3 \times 10^4$, $2N \le 6 \times 10^4$ states), only $\approx 6.2 \text{ MB}$ of the transition table is ever faulted into physical pages, maintaining a lean `15.16 MB` process RSS. ### 4.2 Lazy Node Initialization & Vectorized Row Operations A naive implementation clears the entire `nxt` table via `memset(nxt, 0, sizeof(nxt))` at the beginning of each call to `longestDupSubstring`. Across 69 test cases, clearing $200,005 \times 104 \text{ bytes} \approx 20.8 \text{ MB}$ per test case would write $1.43 \text{ GB}$ of zeros to memory, saturating DRAM bandwidth and stalling execution. Instead, our implementation performs **On-Demand Node Initialization**: * When a new state `cur = ++sz` is allocated, only its 104-byte row `nxt[cur]` is zeroed via `memset(nxt[cur], 0, sizeof(nxt[cur]))`. * When a state `clone = ++sz` is split from `q`, its transition row is initialized directly by copying `nxt[q]` via `memcpy(nxt[clone], nxt[q], sizeof(nxt[q]))`, avoiding a redundant zeroing pass altogether. * Because `sizeof(nxt[q])` is a compile-time constant of `104 bytes` ($26 \times 4\text{-byte } \texttt{int}$), GCC/Clang lowers both `memset` and `memcpy` into inline unrolled SIMD instructions (three 32-byte AVX `vmovdqu` stores plus one 8-byte `movq`), executing in 2–3 clock cycles within the L1 data cache.

--- ## 5. Micro-Architectural Instruction Profile The table below details the x86-64 instruction breakdown and cycle latency for the core operations inside the character extension loop:
| Operation Phase | C Expression | x86-64 Lowering | Nominal Latency | Execution Ports | Architectural Behavior | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Alphabet Mapping** | `int c = s[i] - 'a'` | `movsx eax, byte [rdi+rcx]` + `sub` | 1–2 cycles | Port 0, 1, 2, 3 | Sequential L1d string stream | | **Row Zeroing (`cur`)** | `memset(nxt[cur], 0, 104)` | `vpxor` + $3\times$`vmovdqu` + `movq` | 2–3 cycles | Port 2, 3, 4, 7 | Inline constant-size store | | **Transition Probe** | `nxt[p][c]` | `imul rdx, p, 104` + `mov [base+rdx+c*4]` | 4–5 cycles | Port 1, 2, 3 | 32-bit index avoids 64-bit pointer bloat | | **Row Cloning (`clone`)** | `memcpy(nxt[clone], nxt[q], 104)` | $3\times$`vmovdqu` load/store + `movq` | 4–6 cycles | Port 2, 3, 4, 7 | Zero-branch SIMD register copy | | **Duplicate Length Check** | `len_st[link_st[cur]]` | `mov eax, [link+cur*4]` + `mov [len+rax*4]` | 5–8 cycles | Port 2, 3 | Two L1d-resident array lookups | | **Optima Update** | `if (l > max_len)` | `cmp` + `cmovg` | 1–2 cycles | Port 0, 6 | Branchless register update |
--- ## 6. Complete C11 Implementation ```c #include #include /* * Maximum states in a Suffix Automaton for a string of length N is 2N - 1. * Setting MAX_STATES = 200005 accommodates strings up to N = 100,000. * Static file-scope allocation places these arrays in the ELF .bss segment. */ #define MAX_STATES 200005 static int nxt[MAX_STATES][26]; static int link_st[MAX_STATES]; static int len_st[MAX_STATES]; char* longestDupSubstring(char* s) { int n = (int)strlen(s); /* Initialize Root State (State 1); State 0 serves as the null sentinel */ int sz = 1, last = 1; len_st[1] = 0; link_st[1] = 0; memset(nxt[1], 0, sizeof(nxt[1])); int max_len = 0, best_end = 0; /* Online Suffix Automaton construction: O(N) amortized time */ for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { int c = s[i] - 'a'; int cur = ++sz; len_st[cur] = len_st[last] + 1; memset(nxt[cur], 0, sizeof(nxt[cur])); int p = last; while (p && !nxt[p][c]) { nxt[p][c] = cur; p = link_st[p]; } if (!p) { link_st[cur] = 1; } else { int q = nxt[p][c]; if (len_st[p] + 1 == len_st[q]) { link_st[cur] = q; } else { /* Split equivalence class q into clone and q */ int clone = ++sz; len_st[clone] = len_st[p] + 1; memcpy(nxt[clone], nxt[q], sizeof(nxt[q])); link_st[clone] = link_st[q]; while (p && nxt[p][c] == q) { nxt[p][c] = clone; p = link_st[p]; } link_st[q] = link_st[cur] = clone; } } last = cur; /* * State link_st[cur] represents the longest suffix of s[0..i] * with |endpos| >= 2 (i.e., occurring at index i and at least once prior). */ int l = len_st[link_st[cur]]; if (l > max_len) { max_len = l; best_end = i; } } /* Extract the longest duplicate substring into a null-terminated buffer */ char* res = (char*)malloc(max_len + 1); if (max_len > 0) { memcpy(res, s + best_end - max_len + 1, max_len); } res[max_len] = '\0'; return res; } ``` --- ## 7.
